newsitem.title: UK: Venezuela to export Orimulsion to Italy by early '98.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela to export Orimulsion to Italy by early '98.

text.p: The Venezuelan company Bitor expects to reach agreement on exporting its trademark fuel Orimulsion to Italian electricity firm Enel by early next year, a senior Bitor official said on Tuesday.
Daniel Ramrez-Isava, president of Bitor Europe Ltd, said agreement had been held up because of delays in commissioning the Brndisi South power station which was now expected to open this summer.
Ramrez-Isava told Reuters the brand new plant would burn about two million tonnes a year of Orimulsion if the final negotiations were successful.
He said 500,000 tonnes of Orimulsion would be burnt at the plant over about six months as a test before any long-term deal was signed.
"Final negotiations will be carried out once we have all the data related to the test," he added.
Orimulsion is a controversial fuel that some environmentalists say is extremely dirty, although Bitor denies this.
It is a suspension of naturally occurring bitumen in about 30 percent water and contains toxic heavy metals which Bitor says can be recovered efficiently without escaping into the air.
Bitor had been hoping that a long-term contract with ENEL would be signed early this year, but delays in commissioning the Brndisi plant prevented this.
Ramrez-Isava said Bitor also hoped to begin negotiations on supplying about one million tonnes of Orimulsion a year to the Fiumisanto power station in Sardinia, but this was a longer-term goal.
ENEL has been aiming to reduce its heavy reliance on fuel oil for electricity generation, partly for environmental reasons, and sees Orimulsion and natural gas as alternatives.

Ramrez-Isava said he was optimistic that Britain would import Orimulsion once again, once the go-ahead was given for National Power Plc to convert its 2,000-megawatt Pembroke plant in south Wales to the fuel.
Britain is expected to decide this summer whether to hold a public enquiry into the plant, which would burn four to five million tonnes of Orimulsion a year.
Such an enquiry is expected to last one to two years, but Ramrez-Isava said this would not pose a problem as this possibility had been factored into the planning.
The plant would be fitted with flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) equipment that would remove 94 percent of sulphur dioxide emissions from the combustion gases, according to Bitor.
"We see no reason why it should not be approved," Ramrez-Isava said.
He said nitrogen oxide emissions from Orimulsion plants were 40 percent lower than from coal-fired plants and carbon dioxide emissions were 15 percent lower.
Until last year Britain burnt Orimulsion at two PowerGen Plc plants but these have now been closed.
Ramrez-Isava said the closures were not unexpected as the two plants were not equipped with FGD.
He said he expected a decision in mid-1997 on importing 1.2 million tonnes a year for a planned Turkish plant which would be the first in Europe built specifically to burn Orimulsion.

A feasibility study for the plant, generating 600 megawatts in the initial stages, has been submitted to the Turkish government by U.S. company AES Corp, but Ramrez-Isava said it had not yet been agreed whether it should be developed on the "build, own, operate" or "build, operate, transfer" model.

He also said Bitor and Germany were in their final stages of negotiations on supplying Orimulsion to a coal-fired plant at Ibbenbueren. Orimulsion would replace 20 to 30 per cent of the coal burnt at the plant.

Ramrez-Isava said Bitor was beginning talks with Romania on importing 500,000 tonnes a year and Greece could eventually import one million tonnes annually. In addition a Dutch company could import 200,000 tonnes a year for three cement plants where the limestone produced absorbs sulphur emissions.
Denmark is currently Europe's biggest importer of Orimulsion, consuming 1.5 million tonnes a year.

Other importers include Canada and Japan, while China is involved in a joint study with Bitor on an Orimulsion-producing module in Venezuela and may import five million tonnes a year in three years, Ramrez-Isava said.
Bitor is a subsidiary of state-owned Petrleos de Venezuela SA (PDVSA).
--Michael Rank, London newsroom +44 171 542 4088
